name: principle-prove-it-works
does: Checks the actual feature, data value, full integration path, and delegated artifact before claiming completion; prefers repeatable verification scripts with visible results.
why: Checking the actual result remains useful for your experiments. An additional principle skill adds less than the original rating implied because you already ask for tests and measured outcomes; keep checks proportional to the task.
caveat: Portable prose, but manually invoked in the source. Real scientific effectiveness still needs controlled experiments and uncertainty, not only passing software checks. Chat-reported test results were not independently rerun for this audit.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: principle-redesign-from-first-principles
does: Reconsiders an affected design as though a new requirement existed from the start, propagates it through types and documentation, then delivers incrementally.
why: Reserve for a deliberate redesign. Broad changes would work against your frequent requests to preserve a baseline and vary only one experimental factor.
caveat: Portable and manual. Applying its broad redesign language indiscriminately could invalidate the user's matched DSPy baseline or violate explicit preservation constraints. Reserve for an authorized design change.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state
does: Identifies shared writable files, branches, or state; gives independent workers separate owned outputs; uses locks, single writers, or compare-and-swap only when sharing is essential.
why: Your parallel simulations and visual variants benefit from separate owned outputs. Apply this when workers really share mutable state; it does not need a new workflow on every task.
caveat: Portable and manual. The visual workflow already requests separate variant folders, so some benefit is reinforcement. The sample shows concurrency demand, not proof that existing code has a race.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: principle-sequence-verifiable-units
does: Breaks multi-step edits into checked units and orders commits or PRs to show baseline, failure, and fix instead of checking only after a large batch.
why: Small checked changes can help long experiments, but you already use staged tasks and tests. Additional mandatory checkpoints and commit choreography offer limited net benefit.
caveat: Portable and manual, but the unconditional rebase-to-trunk instruction and failing-test-first commit advice need repository-specific handling. Cheap per-unit checks should not mean rerunning an entire costly battle sweep after every edit.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: principle-subtract-before-you-add
does: Removes dead code, redundant checks, unused features, stub references, and repetitive prompt instructions before adding new complexity.
why: Your tool collection and orchestration prompts are already extensive. Removing unnecessary steps can directly reduce effort, provided experimental baselines, legality checks and reproducibility evidence remain intact.
caveat: Portable and manual. Do not remove legality validation, baseline artifacts, or reproducibility evidence just because they look repetitive; these can be part of the experiment's contract.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: principle-type-system-discipline
does: Uses discriminated variants, semantic brands, constructive data models, boundary parsing, exhaustive matching, and schema-derived types to prevent invalid combinations.
why: Better representations may help typed team schemas, but this is a conditional implementation aid rather than a direct research or learning improvement. Runtime legality checks are still needed.
caveat: Manual; its strongest benefits require a statically checked language. Python annotations or DSPy fields alone do not enforce Pokémon legality, and external model output still needs runtime validation. Sample does not establish prevalence of typed-language work.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: show-me-your-work
does: Keeps an append-only TSV decision log with timestamp, phase, decision, reason, evidence pointer, and result; audits it against the transcript and requires a reviewer from another model family.
why: Your experiments need clear evidence, but a mandatory decision log and additional reviewer create recurring overhead. Save the results and decisions you actually need; do not make the full logging workflow a default.
caveat: Best adapted, not copied unchanged. Source assumes Cursor agent-transcripts paths, a bundled helper/template, and mandatory different-model-family review. Those are not guaranteed in Codex; another GPT variant is not a different family. Its append-only rule also conflicts with later instructions to cut or fix rows.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: swarm
does: Frames a done predicate, fans out N workers for partitioned coverage or a declared race, isolates writable outputs, waits for results, and aggregates PASS/ISSUES/BLOCKED evidence and gaps.
why: Parallel coverage fits your requests, but you already delegate heavily. A separate Cursor-oriented orchestration skill contributes less than clear task boundaries and resource limits in your current tools.
caveat: Cursor-specific cloud-worker arguments and ~/.cursor/rules model configuration are not portable. Default grok-4.5-fast-xhigh is unavailable here. MacBook-only work needs local workers, resource limits, and available Codex tool/model mappings rather than its default cloud fan-out.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: tdd
does: For a cheap, clear bug reproduction, writes and runs a focused failing test before the fix, then verifies passing and adjacent behavior; explicitly permits practical scripted or manual substitutes.
why: Focused regression tests remain useful, but you already have TDD and explicitly request tests when needed. Installing another same-name skill would add overlap and selection ambiguity.
caveat: Portable and manual. This is not a full feature-development TDD replacement and does not by itself establish scientific correctness. Same-name installation creates selection ambiguity with existing tdd skills.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: teach
does: Combines actual how and why skill investigations into a plain explanation at the learner's pace, starts with a small complete answer, preserves uncertainty, and builds diagrams one component at a time.
why: You repeatedly want to understand how something works, not just receive an artifact. This can improve paced explanations of your own code; it is not a complete paper-study or flashcard curriculum and should complement your existing teaching tools.
caveat: Source is primarily code/subsystem teaching, not a paper-reading or practice-exercise curriculum. It depends on how, why, unslop, and sometimes image generation. Full why investigations can be costly. Historical prompts name Matt Pocock teach, but that alone does not prove the skill is currently installed.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: technical-writing
does: Chooses tutorial, how-to, reference, or explanation, then applies reader-focused sentences, short unambiguous instructions, stable terminology, real symbols, and reproducible counts.
why: Your blog, research explanations and concise task prompts are recurring deliverables. Clearer organization and terminology improve those outputs directly, with less setup than maintaining a new verification system.
caveat: Mostly portable and manual; depends on unslop. Treat rigid one-mode-per-document and sentence-length rules as editing aids for scientific blog posts, not reasons to split useful explanations or suppress uncertainty. It does not supply source checking.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: typescript-best-practices
does: Applies type-system discipline in TypeScript with discriminated unions, branded primitives, unknown inputs, validated narrowing, exhaustive checks, schema-derived types, real tests, and structured diagnostics.
why: Conditional on substantial TypeScript work. The observed experiments are largely Python, and type-system guidance is already available; prioritize it only for an actual frontend implementation need.
caveat: Conditional recommendation for actual TypeScript projects. Relies on principle-type-system-discipline, boundary guidance, and referenced examples. Broad 'every as is a crash waiting' wording overstates TypeScript's legitimate assertion use; adapt to project conventions.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: unslop
does: Edits writing for specificity and human voice by removing puffery, vague attribution, repetitive synonyms, canned phrasing, decorative formatting, and dense passive prose.
why: Direct, specific writing helps your prompts and blog. Much is already covered by current writing instructions, so use it as a targeted editing pass rather than another always-on requirement.
caveat: Portable prose, but its 'must always apply' claim and blanket punctuation bans should not override user style, exact quotations, scientific terms, or calibrated uncertainty. Removing AI tells does not verify truth.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.

name: why
does: Anchors a design question in code/history, investigates seven available evidence categories in parallel, and synthesizes direct findings, inferences, competing hypotheses, and explicit gaps with citations.
why: Understanding the reason behind a code decision can help you choose the next change. Use a scoped investigation; the full multi-source orchestration is often excessive, and performance causes still require experiments.
caveat: Heavy Cursor-specific orchestration assumes Grok investigators, a Claude synthesizer, several reference files, and enterprise MCP categories often irrelevant or unavailable for a personal research project. A null search is not proof a decision was never ticketed. Code rationale investigation also cannot replace ablations to establish why DiBO performs worse.
revisionBasis: Reassessed using the user's feedback as a preference for useful outcomes over additional process; this broader preference is an inference.
